clue.text: Incisive critic now in muddles, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of now in muddles are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sharp reviewer finds himself, sadly, in a series of muddles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges NOWINMUDDLES. Edmund Wilson was a leading American literary critic, famously cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Wilson was a sharp-tongued American literary reviewer, so an incisive critic describes him.

clue.text: German town has points for ascetic sectarians

parts.note: Essen is an industrial town in the Ruhr, Germany
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: A town in Germany is said to contain the points of view of a strict religious group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'points' are compass points, a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes were a Jewish religious sect of the Second Temple period living austere communal lives.

clue.text: Short-term employment for a creature of Burns

parts.note: a mo is a short moment of time, a short term
use means employment, as in putting something to use

explanation.surface: A temporary job is offered to one of the animals in Robert Burns's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns addressed a field creature in his poem 'To a Mouse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns wrote the famous poem 'To a Mouse', so the small rodent is his creature.

clue.text: Nothing adequately described their beliefs

parts.note: people who believe in nothing at all: their creed is exactly 'nothing', from Latin nihil

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests words failing to describe a creed; read literally, 'nothing' is the whole of the creed.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of a philosophy rejecting all values and beliefs hold, in effect, a belief in nothing.

clue.text: Architect in some low rent accommodation The contemplative man's companion

indicators.note: accommodation is something that houses, so the phrase low rent houses the answer within it

explanation.surface: An architect lives in some cheap rented housing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral. The text as held runs on into the next clue's words.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Wren was the English designer of St Paul's Cathedral and many London churches.

clue.text: The contemplative man's companion

parts.note: Milton's pensive poem Il Penseroso, the contemplative man, has a twin poem about the cheerful man

explanation.walkthrough: Milton wrote two paired poems: 'Il Penseroso' (the thoughtful man) and its companion piece on the merry man.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's poem of the cheerful man was written as the paired companion to Il Penseroso, the pensive man.

clue.text: Circle bit of abstract style

parts.note: a circle is shaped like the letter O
a part is a bit of something

explanation.surface: A ring forms a fragment of some abstract design.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is an abstract movement of the 1960s using optical illusions.

clue.text: Different readings via second thought, or via rum, perhaps

indicators.note: a second thought rearranges one's first ideas, so the letters of or via are reordered

explanation.surface: Rethinking a text by way of rum, perhaps, yields alternative versions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second thought' rearranges OR VIA into VARIO; 'perhaps' marks the clue's mix of words as playful, and rum is kept as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A variorum edition prints the variant readings of a text along with commentators' notes.

clue.text: A north-eastern sea, very stormy, reveals Trojan prince

indicators.note: a very stormy sea is churned up, so the letters of NE and sea are tossed about

explanation.surface: A rough sea in the north-east uncovers a prince of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very stormy' rearranges NESEA into ENEAS, after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Virgil's Aeneid was a royal Trojan, son of Anchises and Venus.

clue.text: Orientation fit for ordained poet

parts.note: south is a compass direction, one orientation
fit and well both mean healthy

explanation.surface: A direction healthy enough for a poet who took holy orders.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Southwell was an Elizabethan Jesuit priest and poet, executed in 1595.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Southwell was an Elizabethan Jesuit priest who wrote religious verse such as 'The Burning Babe'.

clue.text: An opening for another incisive critic ()

parts.note: a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: An opportunity for yet another sharp reviewer.
explanation.walkthrough: James Agate was a pungent British drama critic of the Sunday Times; 'another' links to 1-across.
explanation.definitionFit: James Agate was a sharp British theatre reviewer of the interwar years.

clue.text: The point of very early comedy

definitions.text: The point of very early comedy

parts.words: The point of very early comedy
parts.note: the sharp object whose loss drives the plot of Gammer Gurton's play, one of the first English comedies

explanation.walkthrough: 'The point' seems to mean the purpose; it is a sharp sewing point, the lost object in 'Gammer Gurton's Needle'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewing pin with an eye is lost and found in Gammer Gurton's comedy, among the earliest in English.

clue.text: Hero's cousin to overcome Osborne's hero

parts.note: to beat is to overcome
Archie Rice is the hero of John Osborne's play The Entertainer

explanation.surface: Literary heroes compete as one cousin beats another playwright's leading man.
explanation.walkthrough: Hero is a character in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, not a heroic figure.
explanation.definitionFit: In Much Ado About Nothing the witty Beatrice is the cousin of the young lady Hero.

clue.text: Cruelty of hell contained in missile

indicators.note: contained in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: SAM is a surface-to-air missile
Dis is the classical underworld, hell

explanation.surface: Hellish cruelty is packed into a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis is the Roman name for the underworld and its god, a classical stand-in for hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadism is delight in inflicting pain, a form of deliberate brutality.

clue.text: All is up to doctor at university to restore Caligula's sister

parts.note: U stands for university

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the words all is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: It falls to a university doctor to bring back the Roman emperor's sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ALL IS into SILLA; the clue's 'to' means this is added to the doctor and university pieces. Drusilla was later deified by her brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Julia Drusilla was the favourite sister of the Roman emperor Gaius, known as Caligula.

clue.text: Dobson's were in China

parts.note: Austin Dobson's verse collection was titled as sayings 'in Porcelain', china being porcelain not the country

explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country; it is porcelain, from Dobson's 'Proverbs in Porcelain' (1877).
explanation.definitionFit: Austin Dobson published a collection called 'Proverbs in Porcelain', so his wise sayings were in china.

clue.text: American money I invested in Spanish wine for Chapman's prince

indicators.note: invested in means the money is put inside the wine

parts.note: vino is Spanish for wine
a cent is a unit of US currency

explanation.surface: A dollar sum is sunk into Spanish wine for a prince in a Chapman play.
explanation.walkthrough: Vincentio is a stock prince's name in Elizabethan drama; the clue points to George Chapman's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Vincentio is a princely character in a play by the Elizabethan dramatist George Chapman.

clue.text: Stevenson heroine in tattered raincoat

indicators.note: something tattered is torn to pieces, so the letters of raincoat are rearranged

explanation.surface: A heroine of Robert Louis Stevenson wears a ragged mac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tattered' rearranges RAINCOAT. 'Catriona' is Stevenson's 1893 sequel to Kidnapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Catriona Drummond is the title heroine of Stevenson's sequel to Kidnapped.

clue.text: Not Chesterton's Man Friday

parts.note: Chesterton's anarchist novel names its hero after the day before Friday: The Man Who Was ...

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man Friday' evokes Robinson Crusoe; in Chesterton's 'The Man Who Was Thursday' the hero is named for a weekday, but not Friday.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's 1908 novel is The Man Who Was Thursday, its title character not named after Friday.

clue.text: Clough describes two of sail at dawn of day

definitions.text: Clough describes two of sail at dawn of day

parts.words: Clough describes two of sail at dawn of day
parts.note: a quotation from Clough's poem 'Qua cursum ventus', with the missing word filled in: two tall ships seen as tall structures of canvas

explanation.walkthrough: The line from Arthur Hugh Clough's poem reads 'Two towers of sail at dawn of day'; the gap printed as a dash is lost from the text as held.
explanation.definitionFit: Clough likens two ships under full canvas to tall structures, the missing word in his line.

clue.text: Pithy, like garden feature?

definitions.meaning: as if resembling a little garden statue of a bearded dwarf, gnome plus the adjective ending -ic

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke second reading: gnome-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnomic means full of short wise sayings, maxims, and jokingly 'like a garden gnome'.

clue.text: He planned to give Parliament a lift

definitions.text: He planned to give Parliament a lift

parts.words: He planned to give Parliament a lift
parts.note: the leader of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot, which aimed to blow Parliament sky-high

explanation.walkthrough: 'a lift' sounds like a kindness; it means blowing it up. Robert Catesby led the Gunpowder Plot of 1605.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Catesby masterminded the 1605 conspiracy to blow up the House of Lords.

clue.text: A scholar for Meredith's Clara, very little in favour of diamonds

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount
for means in favour of
D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games

explanation.surface: A scholarly suitor for Meredith's heroine cares little for jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: In Meredith's 'The Egoist' Clara Middleton finally chooses the scholar Vernon Whitford.
explanation.definitionFit: Vernon Whitford, the bookish cousin in Meredith's The Egoist, wins Clara Middleton's hand.

clue.text: Stuff of comedy

definitions.meaning: to stuff, as in filling a bird with forcemeat (an old cookery sense)

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for comic material; read separately, an old verb for stuffing poultry and a type of comic play.
explanation.definitionFit: Farce comes from French farcir, to fill with forcemeat, and also names broad knockabout drama.

clue.text: Children's writer in Braine's biting satire

indicators.note: in means the answer lies inside the words Braine's biting

explanation.surface: An author for the young turns up in John Braine's sharp satire.
explanation.walkthrough: E. Nesbit wrote The Railway Children; John Braine wrote Room at the Top.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Nesbit wrote The Railway Children and Five Children and It.

clue.text: Close thy —, open thy Goethe " (Carlyle, Sartor Resartus) ()

definitions.text: Close thy —, open thy Goethe " (Carlyle, Sartor Resartus)

parts.words: Close thy —, open thy Goethe " (Carlyle, Sartor Resartus)
parts.note: Carlyle urges readers to put down the gloomy Romantic poet of Childe Harold and take up Goethe

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-gap quotation from Carlyle's Sartor Resartus: 'Close thy Byron; open thy Goethe.'
explanation.definitionFit: Carlyle contrasts Goethe with the brooding English Romantic author of Childe Harold.

clue.text: Melville skipper, ever unreliable

indicators.note: something unreliable cannot be relied on to stay put, so the letters of ever shift

explanation.surface: A Melville sea captain is never to be trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Vere commands HMS Bellipotent in Melville's 'Billy Budd'.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain the Honourable Edward Fairfax Vere is the ship's captain in Melville's Billy Budd.

clue.text: The one of the Queen's navy was once a window cleaner ()

definitions.text: The one of the Queen's navy was once a window cleaner

parts.words: The one of the Queen's navy was once a window cleaner
parts.note: Sir Joseph Porter in HMS Pinafore sings that he cleaned windows as a lad and rose to head the Queen's Navee

explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, Sir Joseph sings 'Now I am the ruler of the Queen's Navee' after recalling cleaning the windows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Joseph Porter, the First Lord of the Admiralty in HMS Pinafore, calls himself the head of the Queen's Navee.

clue.text: Leonora, Leonora, Leonora

parts.note: Beethoven wrote three Leonore curtain-raisers, numbered 1 to 3, for his opera Fidelio

explanation.walkthrough: Leonora looks like a name called three times; Beethoven's three Leonore preludes for his opera are the reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's three Leonore pieces are orchestral preludes written for his opera Fidelio.

clue.text: Shire of sorceress remembered by

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Shire of sorceress remembered by (12)' is cut short: the cross-reference (presumably to 1-across, Edmund Wilson's Memoirs of Hecate County) that the definition needs is missing
